quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on resultant counts, hank prices and why counts cannot simply be averaged.

questions.q: Why can two Ne counts not be averaged directly to get the count of the yarns together?
options: Because Ne is an indirect number; what adds is the weight per hank, not the count
Because Ne is a direct number and weights are not additive
Because counts can only be added, never averaged
Because yarn prices interfere with the count
questions.explain: Ne measures length per weight, so weights per hank (1/Ne) add, and the mean must be taken of the reciprocals. Averaging the counts themselves overstates the fineness.

questions.q: The resultant count of two singles twisted into a plied yarn is:
options: Equal to the sum of the two counts
questions.explain: The plied yarn carries the weight of both singles per unit length, so it is coarser than either and its Ne is lower than both.

questions.q: The mean count of two yarns running side by side (not twisted) lies:
questions.explain: The mean count of n yarns together is n ÷ Σ(1/N), which always falls between the smallest and largest count, though slightly below the arithmetic average.

questions.q: A hank in this lecture is a length of:
questions.explain: The Ne system uses an 840-yd hank; hank price is the price of 840 yd of the yarn.

questions.q: The hank price of a yarn is its price per 10 lb divided by 10 and by its Ne.
questions.explain: Price per 10 lb ÷ 10 is the price per pound; a pound contains Ne hanks, so dividing again by Ne gives the price of one hank.

questions.q: Twisting Ne 7 and Ne 10 together gives a plied count of about:
questions.explain: Mean count = 2 ÷ (1/7 + 1/10) = 8.24; plied count = 8.24 ÷ 2 = 4.12. The simple average route gives 4.25, which is wrong.

questions.q: For yarns of equal count, the plied count of n singles is:
options: The single count divided by n
The single count multiplied by n
The single count divided by 2 regardless of n
questions.explain: Equal counts give a mean equal to the single count, and plying divides by n; e.g. three Ne 30 singles make a 3-ply of Ne 10.

questions.q: The difference between the true mean count and the simple average of the counts grows as the two counts move further apart.
questions.explain: The lecture notes this: for Ne 7 and 10 the gap is 8.24 versus 8.5; for Ne 10 and 40 the true mean is 16 while the simple average is 25.

questions.q: The price of a yarn mixture per 10 lb is found as:
questions.explain: Mean hank price × mean count gives the price per pound (there are mean-count hanks in a pound); × 10 gives the price per 10 lb.

questions.q: In the lecture, which quantity is averaged to find the price of the mix?
questions.explain: Each yarn's price per 10 lb is converted into a price per hank, the hank prices are averaged, and the result is multiplied back by the mean count. Averaging prices per 10 lb would ignore the different weights of the yarns.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: The mean-count and plied-count formulas, the hank-price route and how results move when one count changes.

questions.q: The mean count of n yarns running together is:
questions.explain: The reciprocals 1/N are weights per hank and add; n divided by their sum is the mean count. The arithmetic average (first option) is the common wrong answer.

questions.q: Twisted (plied) count equals:
questions.explain: The plied yarn is n times heavier per unit length than the mean single, so its count is the mean count divided by n.

questions.q: For two yarns, the resultant plied count can also be written as:
questions.explain: 2 ÷ (1/N₁ + 1/N₂) = 2N₁N₂ ÷ (N₁ + N₂) is the mean; dividing by 2 gives the plied count N₁N₂ ÷ (N₁ + N₂). For Ne 7 and 10: 70 ÷ 17 = 4.12.

questions.q: If yarn 2 is made coarser (lower Ne) while yarn 1 stays the same, the mean count:
questions.explain: A coarser yarn adds more weight per hank, so 1/N₂ grows, the denominator grows and the mean count falls.

questions.q: The hank price of a yarn rises when its Ne rises, other things equal.
questions.explain: Hank price = price per 10 lb ÷ 10 ÷ Ne; a finer yarn gives more hanks per pound, so each hank costs less for the same price per pound.

questions.q: Two yarns have the same price per 10 lb but different counts. Which has the higher hank price?
questions.explain: At the same price per pound the coarser yarn has fewer hanks in a pound, so each hank costs more.

questions.q: Price of a plied yarn per 10 lb compared with the same yarns run together is:
options: Lower by the twist cost only
questions.explain: In the worksheet both figures are Rs 521.76: twisting changes the count but not the weight of yarn bought per 10 lb, so the yarn price per 10 lb is unchanged (twisting cost itself is not included here).

questions.q: Three equal singles of Ne N plied together give a resultant count of:
questions.explain: Mean count stays N; plied count = N ÷ n = N ÷ 3. For Ne 30 singles the 3-ply is Ne 10.

questions.q: Price per 10 lb of a mixture = mean hank price × mean count × 10.
questions.explain: Hanks per pound = mean count; price per pound = mean hank price × mean count; × 10 converts to 10 lb.

questions.q: If both hank prices rise by 10 % and the counts are unchanged, the price of the mix per 10 lb:
questions.explain: The mean hank price rises 10 % and the mean count is unchanged, so the product rises 10 %.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Mean counts, plied counts, hank prices and mixture prices — give answers to two decimal places unless told otherwise.

questions.q: Ne 20 and Ne 30 run together. What is the mean count?
Ne 20 and Ne 30 are twisted into a two-ply yarn. What is the resultant count?
questions.explain: Mean count 24 ÷ 2 = Ne 12; equivalently 20 × 30 ÷ (20 + 30) = 12.

questions.q: Ne 7 and Ne 10 run together. Give the mean count to two decimal places.
questions.explain: 1/7 + 1/10 = 0.2429; 2 ÷ 0.2429 = 8.24 Ne, the figure in the lecture worksheet.

questions.q: Ne 20, Ne 15 and Ne 15 run together. What is the mean count, to two decimal places?
The three yarns Ne 20, Ne 15 and Ne 15 are twisted into one 3-ply yarn. Resultant count, to two decimal places?
questions.explain: Mean count 16.36 ÷ 3 = Ne 5.45.

questions.q: Ne 7 yarn costs Rs 397 per 10 lb. What is its hank price, to three decimal places?
questions.explain: Rs 397 ÷ 10 = Rs 39.70 per lb; ÷ 7 hanks per lb = Rs 5.671 per hank.

questions.q: A Ne 10 yarn has a hank price of Rs 7.00. What is its price per 10 lb?
questions.explain: Price per lb = hank price × Ne = 7 × 10 = Rs 70; per 10 lb = Rs 700.

questions.q: Two yarns have hank prices Rs 5.00 and Rs 7.00 and a mean count of Ne 24. Price of the mixture per 10 lb?
questions.explain: Mean hank price = (5 + 7) ÷ 2 = Rs 6; × 24 × 10 = Rs 1,440 per 10 lb.

questions.q: Ne 40 and Ne 60 are plied together. The resultant count is:
questions.explain: Mean = 2 ÷ (1/40 + 1/60) = 48; plied = 48 ÷ 2 = Ne 24. Ne 25 is the simple-average error and Ne 48 is the mean without halving.

questions.q: Two singles of Ne 16 are twisted together. The resultant count is:
questions.explain: Equal counts: mean stays Ne 16 and the two-ply is 16 ÷ 2 = Ne 8.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Costing-office situations: quoting plied yarns, comparing suppliers and catching the simple-average mistake.

questions.q: A buyer wants a 2-ply yarn equivalent to Ne 10 single, made from two equal singles. Which single count do you order?
questions.explain: A two-ply of equal singles has half the single count, so two Ne 20 singles give a Ne 10 two-ply.

questions.q: A trainee averages Ne 7 and Ne 10 to Ne 8.5 and quotes a fabric weight on that basis. What goes wrong?
options: The weight is overstated because 8.5 is too coarse
The weight is understated because the true mean count 8.24 is coarser than 8.5
questions.explain: The true mean is Ne 8.24, coarser (heavier) than Ne 8.5, so the fabric would weigh about 3 % more than quoted.

questions.q: Supplier A offers Ne 20 at Rs 600 per 10 lb; supplier B offers Ne 30 at Rs 750 per 10 lb. Which has the cheaper hank price?
options: Supplier A at Rs 3.00 per hank
Supplier B at Rs 2.50 per hank
Supplier B at Rs 3.75 per hank
questions.explain: A: 600 ÷ 10 ÷ 20 = Rs 3.00; B: 750 ÷ 10 ÷ 30 = Rs 2.50 per hank. The finer yarn costs more per pound but gives more length.

questions.q: You mix Ne 20 (Rs 600/10 lb) and Ne 30 (Rs 750/10 lb) in equal threads. What is the price of the mixture per 10 lb?
questions.explain: Hank prices 3.00 and 2.50 average 2.75; mean count = 2 ÷ (1/20 + 1/30) = 24; price = 2.75 × 24 × 10 = Rs 660. Rs 675 is the simple average of the two prices, which ignores the weights.

questions.q: If a mill twists two singles bought at Rs 500 per 10 lb each, the yarn cost of the plied yarn per 10 lb (before twisting charges) is still Rs 500.
questions.explain: Twisting does not change the weight of yarn in 10 lb, only the count, so the yarn cost per 10 lb stays the same; twisting conversion would be added separately.

questions.q: A cord warp runs Ne 10 and Ne 40 side by side. The simple average is Ne 25. The true mean count is:
questions.explain: 2 ÷ (1/10 + 1/40) = 2 ÷ 0.125 = Ne 16. The wide gap between the counts makes the simple average badly wrong.

questions.q: The spinner quotes Rs 5.40 per hank for Ne 15. The costing clerk needs the price per 10 lb. It is:
questions.explain: Rs 5.40 × 15 hanks per lb = Rs 81 per lb; × 10 = Rs 810 per 10 lb.

questions.q: A fancy yarn is made by twisting three singles of Ne 24. The knitter asks for the resultant count. You say:
questions.explain: Three equal singles: mean count Ne 24, plied count 24 ÷ 3 = Ne 8. Ne 12 would be the two-ply.

questions.q: Which of these steps is an error that makes a quoted mixture price too high?
options: Multiplying mean hank price by the simple average of the counts instead of the true mean count
Dividing the price per 10 lb by 10 and by Ne
questions.explain: The simple average of the counts is higher than the true mean count, so it overstates hanks per pound: 6.336 × 8.5 × 10 = Rs 538.6 against the correct 6.336 × 8.24 × 10 = Rs 521.76. The other three steps are all correct parts of the method.

questions.q: A towel border uses one Ne 10 and one Ne 20 thread together in every dent. For yarn-weight purposes the pair behaves like a single yarn of:
questions.explain: Mean count = 2 ÷ (1/10 + 1/20) = 13.33; the plied equivalent would be 6.67 and 15 is the simple average.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Two-step problems and reverse calculations across mean counts, plied counts and hank prices.

questions.q: Two yarns, Ne 7 (Rs 397/10 lb) and Ne 10 (Rs 700/10 lb), run together. Price of the mixture per 10 lb, to the nearest rupee?
A two-ply yarn must come out at Ne 12 and one single is Ne 20. What count must the other single be?
questions.explain: For a two-ply 1/N_ply = 1/N₁ + 1/N₂, so 1/N₂ = 1/12 − 1/20 = 0.0333 and N₂ = Ne 30.

questions.q: Which statement about Ne 7 + Ne 10 is wrong?
options: The plied count is half the mean count
questions.explain: 4.25 comes from halving the simple average 8.5; the correct plied count is 8.24 ÷ 2 = 4.12.

questions.q: Three yarns Ne 20 (Rs 710), Ne 15 (Rs 355) and Ne 15 (Rs 810), prices per 10 lb, run together. Mean hank price, to three decimal places?
questions.explain: Hank prices 3.550, 2.367 and 5.400; their mean is 11.317 ÷ 3 = Rs 3.772.

questions.q: With a mean hank price of Rs 3.772 and a mean count of Ne 16.36, what is the price of the mixture per 10 lb, to the nearest rupee?
Running Ne 10 and Ne 40 together gives a mean count of Ne 16, and plying them gives Ne 8.
questions.explain: 2 ÷ (1/10 + 1/40) = 16 for the mean, and 16 ÷ 2 = 8 for the two-ply — equivalently 10 × 40 ÷ 50 = 8.

questions.q: A Ne 7 yarn and a Ne 10 yarn are run together. What share of the combined weight is the Ne 7 yarn?
questions.explain: Weights per hank are 1/7 = 0.1429 and 1/10 = 0.1; the Ne 7 share is 0.1429 ÷ 0.2429 = 59 %. The coarser yarn always carries more than half the weight.

questions.q: A spinner sells Ne 30 at Rs 2.367 per hank. What is the price per 10 lb, to the nearest rupee?
questions.explain: 2.367 × 30 hanks per lb = Rs 71.01 per lb; × 10 = Rs 710 per 10 lb.

questions.q: Two singles of different counts are plied. A student computes mean count 24, then multiplies by 2 to get the plied count 48. What should he have done?
questions.explain: The plied yarn is heavier, so its count is lower: mean ÷ n = 24 ÷ 2 = Ne 12. Multiplying makes the plied yarn finer than its singles, which is impossible.

questions.q: Four Ne 40 singles are twisted together, then that yarn is plied with one Ne 10 single. Resultant count of the final yarn?
questions.explain: Four Ne 40 singles make Ne 10; two Ne 10 yarns plied give 1 ÷ (1/10 + 1/10) = Ne 5.
